title: One hardship, two eases
hookLine: Surah ash-Sharh: with hardship, ease, said twice
carry: with hardship comes ease, not after it
tomorrow: what do you say the moment you hear someone's gone?

lines: BAD NEWS AND GOOD, SAME HOUR.
cards: Some weeks the bad news and the good news arrive in the same hour. A layoff and a friend's engagement. A hard diagnosis and a baby's first word.
A hospital room, and two old friends laughing over a photo album. It can feel wrong to laugh in a week like that.
The Qur'an has a short surah with one line in it, said twice in a row, word for word, that speaks right to that feeling.

teach.b: It's Surah ash-Sharh, also called al-Inshirah. In Pickthall's words: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." Two things to notice.
First, the word is with, not after. The ease isn't waiting at the end of the tunnel; it's in the tunnel with you. The laugh in the hospital room.
The neighbor who brings food. The nurse who learns your grandmother's name. Second, the repeat.
Commentators point to a detail in the Arabic: hardship has the word the, both times, as if it's the same hardship; ease doesn't, as if there are two.
A saying reported from early Muslims puts it like this: one hardship will not overcome two eases. So the repeat isn't filler. It's a promise, doubled.
And the surah has a story behind it. It came in Mecca, and many commentators read it as comfort for the Prophet ﷺ in hard early years, when few listened and many mocked.
It reminds him of a burden that weighed on his back and was lifted. And it ends by turning him toward action: when you're free, keep striving, and turn your longing to your Lord.
Nothing here pretends the hardship is small.

teach.h: NAMED, AND MET IN THE SAME BREATH.

teach.b: And each time, in the same breath, ease comes with it.

how: Muslims recite Surah ash-Sharh in prayer and recall 'with hardship, ease' in hard times, often reminding one another of it, in Arabic, as fa inna ma'a al-'usri yusra.

o: ease that arrives inside a hard time, not after it
a hardship sent to punish someone who strayed
a hard time that has to end before ease can come

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the ease is inside the hardship

s: 94:5 promises ease once the hardship is over
the word is with: the ease comes with the hardship, inside it.
the line 'with hardship goeth ease' is said twice in a row
94:5 and 94:6; a saying reports: one hardship will not overcome two eases.
the surah ends by telling the Prophet to rest now that his burden is gone
it ends: when you're free, keep striving, and turn your longing to your Lord.

games.q: your friend lost her job the same week her sister got engaged, and she feels guilty for being happy at the party. what fits 94:5–6?
o: the ease came with the hardship; the joy belongs in the same week.
she should hold off celebrating until the job search is over.
the engagement cancels out the job loss, so it all evens out.
games.why: with, not after: the surah puts the ease inside the hardship. it doesn't cancel the hardship, and it doesn't have to wait for it to end.

practice: Bring one hardship you're in right now into view. Don't fix it; just look at it. Then, inside it, find one ease that came with it: a person who showed up, a laugh, a small mercy you almost missed.
Count as many as come, on your fingers, slowly.

wordCard.voice: With hardship: and, in the same breath, ease. Not after it. With it, and said twice.

orig.note: Arabic (94:5): with the hardship, ease; 'the' on hardship, none on ease.

carryVoice: Your line: with hardship comes ease, not after it. It comes inside the hard thing. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease.

sources.ref: Qur'an 94:2–3, 94:7–8 (the burden lifted from his back; when free, strive, and turn to your Lord)
the saying 'one hardship will not overcome two eases' (reported from early Muslims; cited in tafsir of 94:5–6)
